# Welcome {-}

How many patients would make a study informative? This tutorial connects a clinical question to its assumptions, a sample size calculation, and the results that different repetitions of the study could produce.

The aims of this module are to understand the importance of recruiting an appropriate number of patients into your study and to be able to calculate the required sample size given reasonable assumptions when designing your study. This open edition retains the questions and clinical narrative of the original tutorial dated **14 May 2021** [@tamasi2021], with additional explanations and browser activities.

The [Introduction](#clinical-question) focuses on **two-arm randomized controlled clinical trials**. The treatment-comparison examples use two independent groups with equal allocation, a binary or continuous outcome, and a two-sided comparison. Later sections broaden the discussion to precision, prevalence surveys and pilot feasibility studies; [Where does my study fit?](#study-designs) guides you to methods for other designs. A single-mean example illustrates [Type I error rate](#alpha), [Type II error rate](#beta) and [power](#statistical-power) using a known population SD. All numerical cases are hypothetical teaching examples. Further background comes from lecture notes by @clayton2019 and the medical introductions by @kirkwood2003, @whitley2002, @pourhoseingholi2013 and @wang2020.

The presentation and three simulation activities are inspired by chapters 1, 11 and 15 of *Power Analysis with Superpower* [@superpowerbook2022]. The clinical explanations, activities and figures here are tailored to this tutorial.

Teaching material is shared under CC BY 4.0 and original code under MIT. You may reuse and adapt the material with attribution. The [teaching guide](../teaching/TEACHING_GUIDE.md), [case template](../case-studies/student_case_template.md) and [assessment rubric](../teaching/assessment_rubric.md) support classroom use. Public attribution or publication requires consent.

## How to use this tutorial {-}

Read the question, make a prediction, inspect the output, and explain what it means for the clinical study. Hover over a figure or table reference, or use its **Preview** button, to inspect it while reading. R code and raw console output are collapsed initially: select **R code and output** to inspect them. Formatted results, tables and figures remain visible. Each chapter offers HTML and PDF downloads; HTML retains the expandable explanations and code, while PDF expands the teaching explanations and keeps technical code hidden. Lines starting with `#` inside code are comments; `##` marks console output, and `[1]` identifies the first printed element of an R output. Select an amber **Common misconception** title to read its explanation.

Open [the tutorial and matching app together](http://127.0.0.1:8769/study/?activity=pain_one_many) for the guided activities. Each activity link loads the same case and assumptions used in the text. The [Sample size reasoning lab](http://127.0.0.1:8769/power_explorer/) is also available on its own. The prepared figures and results in this tutorial provide a route without the app. Other [clinical sample size tools](http://127.0.0.1:8769/apps.html) cover two proportions, two means and dropout.

For a reminder of a term, see [Key parameters and prerequisites](#glossary). If you are applying the material to your own project, begin with [Where does my study fit?](#study-designs) and [Plan your own study](#own-study). [Common mistakes and questions](#common-mistakes) collects explanations you can return to while working.

Need help finding your way around? See [Using the toolbar](#using-the-toolbar) below.

By the end, you should be able to:

- Choose a testing, estimation or fixed-resource planning goal and explain why it fits the question.
- Distinguish expected effects, planning effects and clinically meaningful thresholds.
- Justify assumptions and examine plausible alternatives, including when reusing an existing dataset.
- Explain Type I error rate, Type II error rate and power, and why one study can be inconclusive despite high planned power.
- Calculate approximate sample sizes for two means or two proportions, and plan the precision of a single-proportion estimate.
- Read power curves and distinguish per-group, total, analysable and recruitment counts.
- Interpret repeated-study rejection, coverage, precision and Monte Carlo uncertainty.
- Interpret an interval against zero and a clinical threshold, and recognise when a study design needs another planning method.
- Write a study justification that records evidence, assumptions, sensitivity, feasibility and limitations, and reproduce its calculations.
